title: One red main, one fixer

story: Tuesday, 10:02. A pull request is merged into main, and with it comes a small change that breaks a unit test in the projects table. Main's frontend CI goes red. A red build on main is exactly what our CI fixer is for: a routine, which means the same agent as Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, but started by a red build instead of a ticket. So a fixer wakes up.

At 10:05 a teammate merges something unrelated, and that build is red too, on the same test, because main is still broken. By 10:31 five builds have failed the same way. If each red build wakes its own fixer, we get five agents writing the same one-line fix and five pull requests for one broken test, and someone has to close four of them by hand.
hook.question: How do we get exactly one fixer per problem, however many builds go red?

play.intro: Seven red builds came in between 10:02 and 10:31: five on the same broken test, one lint error and one type error. Choose what goes into the fingerprint and what to strip from the error line, and aim for exactly three fixers. Guess before each run.

tasks.text: Hash each build as it is: last green commit, job name and the raw first error line. How many fixers start?
Strip only the timestamps. Does that bring the five test failures together?
Strip timestamps, temp paths and run numbers. How many fixers now?
Add the pushed commit "to be safe". What happens to the fixers, and to the bill?
Turn off the first error line but keep the job names. Why does one fixer now get two different problems?

read.h: Name the problem, not the build
p: When main breaks, every later build on main fails for the same reason until someone fixes it. The trigger service, our small service that hears about red builds, turns each of those builds into a workflow ID, and that ID decides everything: Temporal allows one open run per ID, so builds with the same ID share one fixer. Name the run after the build and every red build gets its own fixer. Name it after the problem and they all share one.

To name the problem, we keep only what stays the same while main is broken. The last green commit is the newest commit where this CI workflow passed on main, and it does not move until main is fixed. The failing job names say where it broke, and each job's first error line says what broke. We need the error line as well as the job name, because one job, such as a check job that runs both the linter and the type checker, can fail for two unrelated reasons. Before hashing, we normalise the error line, which means we strip the timestamp, the temporary folder and the duration. Those change on every run even when the failure is exactly the same.

notes.text: The first log line that mentions an error or a failure. Later lines are usually consequences of it.
Timestamps in both forms that show up in CI logs: 2026-10-14T10:01:22.2113356Z and 2026-10-14 11:20:15.668.
Temporary folders such as /tmp/ci-8sK2pq get a new random name on every run.
Durations such as 48ms or 1.2s. The same failing test is faster or slower each time.
Sorted, so the order in which jobs failed does not change the fingerprint.
The pushed commit is left out on purpose: it is new on every push, so it would give every build its own fixer.

read.h: Tell the open run, or start it
p: Now each red build has a name for its problem, and the trigger service must hand it to Temporal. You already know the plain start call with the conflict policy USE_EXISTING: a second start with the same ID gets a handle to the open run instead of making a new one. That is enough for a ticket, where a second trigger brings nothing new. A red build is different. It is fresh evidence that the problem is still there, with a log the fixer may want to read, and a start that only joins delivers none of it.

signalWithStart solves this in one call. A signal is a message to a running workflow. If a run with this ID is open, signalWithStart delivers the signal to it; if none is open, it starts the run and then delivers the signal. Our signal is called addTrigger, and its message is the red build. Either way the build reaches the one run. And because Temporal does both steps as one operation, two builds that arrive at the same moment still cannot start two runs.

notes.text: routineRun is the workflow every routine runs, the CI fixer included.
The signal, with the red build as its message. An open run receives it; a new run receives it right after it starts.
What happens when this ID's run has already closed. The last section explains it.

read.h: Wait for the storm to gather
p: Red builds do not arrive together. On Tuesday they came over half an hour, because each one waits for someone to merge and for CI to finish. If the fixer started work the moment its run started, it would plan from the first build alone and hold a machine while the rest of the evidence was still on its way.

So routineRun, the workflow every routine runs, first sleeps through a gather window, which is seven minutes for red main. The sleep is a Temporal timer, so the run holds no machine and the timer survives a restart of our worker. The addTrigger handler keeps working during the sleep, so every build that arrives lands in the list. When the window ends, the run checks that main is still red at its latest commit (if someone reverted the change in the meantime, it ends with nothing to do), passes its safety gates, and only then claims a VM.

notes.text: Every red build that arrives as a signal is pushed here, also while the run sleeps.
Routines started by a ticket or a schedule get their one trigger in the input instead of by signal.
The gather window. The CI fixer's charter, the routine's short settings file, sets gather_minutes to 7; a bug fixer sets none and starts at once.
The safety gates: the kill switch, a paused routine, incident mode and one open PR per routine. A later lesson covers them. A gate that says wait never claims a VM.

read.h: When the same problem comes back
p: A fixer run ends: it opened its pull request, or it found nothing to do. By default a closed run frees its name, as you saw for tickets. For red main that default would be a mistake, and the fingerprint shows why. It contains the last green commit, so if the fix worked and main went green, any new break gets a new fingerprint. The same fingerprint can only come back if main has not been green since its run closed, which means the fix did not hold or never landed. Another fixer with the same evidence would probably try the same fix again, and two fixers can end up undoing each other in what people call ping-pong.

So the call sets the reuse policy, the setting that decides whether an ID can be used again after its run closed, to REJECT_DUPLICATE. Temporal then refuses to start a closed ID again and throws WorkflowExecutionAlreadyStartedError. The trigger service catches exactly that error and posts the problem to #ai-agents-alerts, our Slack channel for platform alerts, where a person takes over. Temporal remembers a closed ID for as long as it keeps the run's history, which is 30 days in our Temporal.

notes.text: Only this refusal is expected. Any other error is a real failure and is thrown again.

deeper.h: Go deeper: how a red build reaches the trigger service
p: In the product repo, a small GitHub Actions workflow listens for workflow_run, the event GitHub sends when another workflow finishes. When one of the CI workflows fails on main, or on a renovate/ branch where Renovate, our dependency-update bot, opens its PRs, this workflow runs on our own self-hosted runners inside our internal cluster and posts only the run's ID and repo to the trigger service. It holds no secret. It proves who it is with a GitHub OIDC token, a short-lived note signed by GitHub that says which repo and workflow is calling. It never checks out code, so nothing from a branch can run there.

The trigger service trusts nothing in that request except where to look. It reads the run again from GitHub through the broker, the service that holds our GitHub credentials, and gets the failing jobs and their logs itself. Only then does it compute the fingerprint. A failed Renovate PR gets a simpler name, upgrade:fcp:pr- and the PR number, because the PR already names the problem.

Two other kinds of trigger start routines without a fingerprint. A poll asks Jira every five minutes for triaged Bug tickets and starts a bug fixer run named after the ticket, the same way Nova's runs are named. Temporal schedules start the daily and weekly routines, each named sched: and the schedule's name. In both cases the name already says what the work is, so a plain start that joins is enough.

lab.title: One red main, one fixer
lab.goal: Give every red build a fingerprint of its problem, so that all the builds that are red for the same reason join one fixer run, and builds with different problems never share one.

guess.q: Main went red because of one broken test, and then 5 people pushed. All 5 builds fail on that same test. If the fixer's workflow ID is cifix:fcp:<hash of the whole failure record>, how many fixer runs start?

options.text: 1, because it is the same problem.
options.why: The record also holds the run id, the start time and the pushed commit, and they change on every build, so the 5 hashes are all different.
Every record is a little different, so every hash is different, and Temporal sees 5 different IDs: a storm of fixers.

options.text: 0, because Temporal refuses to start the same thing twice.
options.why: Temporal only joins or refuses runs with the same ID. These 5 IDs are different, so to Temporal they are 5 different things.

lab.build: Open fingerprint.mjs and write three small functions. firstError(log) gives back the first line that says error or fail. normalise(line) removes what changes on every run: timestamps (in both formats), temp folders like /tmp/ci-8sK2pq, and durations like 48ms or 1.2s. fingerprint(failure) hashes lastGreenSha plus one line per failing job, "job name | normalised first error", sorted, and gives back the first 12 hex characters. Run node storm.mjs until it says 7 red builds on main → 3 fixer runs, then run ./academy check, which also tries 3 red builds you have not seen.
lab.fix: Last night someone wanted "more precise" fixers, so they added the pushed commit to the fingerprint. This morning main went red, ten people pushed, and ten fixer runs started on the same broken test, each one with its own PR. Run node storm.mjs --fix to see the storm, then repair fix/fingerprint.mjs.
explain: Why does the fixer's workflow ID come from a fingerprint of the problem, and not from the build that failed?
Name two things you strip before hashing and two things you keep. Why does each one belong on its side?
Main turned green again, and an hour later the same test broke again. Should that start a new fixer, or join the old one? Why?
lab.done: node storm.mjs shows 7 red builds on main → 3 fixer runs, and ./academy check passes, also on the hidden builds.

check.q: Why does the fingerprint leave out the commit that was pushed?

options.text: Commit hashes are too long to hash again
options.why: Length does not matter to a hash function. The problem is what the commit means, not its size.

options.text: Every push has a new commit, so including it gives every red build its own fingerprint and its own fixer
options.why: The fingerprint must be the same for every build that is red for the same reason. The pushed commit changes with every push, so it brings the storm back.

options.text: The pushed commit is not known when the build fails
options.why: It is known: every build records the commit it ran on. We leave it out on purpose.

check.q: The trigger service could call start with USE_EXISTING instead of signalWithStart. Both give one run per fingerprint. What do we lose?

options.text: The later red builds: they join the run, but their details never reach it
options.why: A start that joins only returns a handle. signalWithStart also delivers each build to the run as an addTrigger signal, so the fixer sees all the evidence.

options.text: The protection against duplicates, because start would make a second run
options.why: USE_EXISTING joins the open run, so there is still only one run. The difference is the message, not the count.

options.text: Nothing; signalWithStart is just a shorter way to write the same call
options.why: They behave differently: only signalWithStart carries a message into the run.

check.q: The run cifix:fcp:3fa91c27d0e4 closed an hour ago, but main never went green. A new red build has the same fingerprint. What does REJECT_DUPLICATE make happen?

options.text: A new run starts with the same ID and tries again
options.why: That is the default reuse policy, ALLOW_DUPLICATE. We switch it off here because a second try would likely repeat the first.

options.text: The build is added to the closed run as a signal
options.why: Only open runs receive signals. A closed run cannot be joined.

options.text: Temporal refuses the start, and the trigger service posts the problem to the alerts channel for a person
options.why: The same fingerprint after its run closed means the fix did not hold. The refusal turns that into an alert instead of another fixer.

p: In our platform the trigger service lives in the orchestrator on inf-rhinohealth, behind an internal POST /v1/events route, so there is still no public webhook. A small Action in fcp, ai-agents-routine-trigger.yml on fcp-runner-set, calls it with a GitHub OIDC token whenever [FRONTEND] - CI, [CLOUD] - CI, [CLIENT] - CI or [SDK] - CI fails on main or on a renovate/ branch. Red main signals or starts cifix:fcp:<fingerprint> on the ai-agents-cifix queue; a failed Renovate PR uses upgrade:fcp:pr-<n>.

Every routine runs the same workflow, routineRun. It reuses ticketToPr's activities and shares the PR half, shipPr, with Nova, so the walls and review layers are built once. Bug tickets and schedules reach it another way: the bug poll uses Nova's Jira poll registry every 5 minutes and starts bugfix:RH-1240 through startRun, and the daily and weekly crews are Temporal schedules named sched:<name> with overlap SKIP.

tickets.why: routineRun itself: the addTrigger signal, the gather-window sleep, and the gates before any VM.
The heart of this lesson: the fingerprint, signalWithStart, and REJECT_DUPLICATE with the alert.
The small Action in fcp that reports a red build with an OIDC token, and does nothing else.
The triggers that need no fingerprint: the Jira bug poll and the Temporal schedules.

words.plain: A short code made from what stays the same while main is broken. Same problem, same code, same run.
The newest commit on main where this CI workflow passed. It does not move while main stays red.
Strip the parts of an error line that change on every run, such as timestamps and temporary folders.
One call that sends a signal to the open run with this ID, or starts the run and then sends the signal.
The minutes a fixer run waits before working, so all the red builds of one storm land in it. Seven for red main.
A reuse policy: an ID whose run has closed may not start again.

review.q: From memory: the three parts of the fingerprint, and three things normalising strips from the error line.
review.a: The last green commit, the failing job names, and each job's first error line. Normalising strips timestamps, temporary folders and durations (and anything else that changes per run, like a run number). The pushed commit is never part of it.

review.q: A teammate wants to remove the gather window "so fixes start faster". What do you answer?
review.a: Red builds arrive over many minutes. Without the window the fixer plans from the first build and holds a VM while the rest of the evidence is still arriving. The seven minutes cost no machine, because a sleeping run holds none.

review.q: Main has been red for two hours on the same test, and the alerts channel says the CI fixer's problem came back. What happened, and what do you look at first?
review.a: The fixer's run closed, but main never went green, so the same fingerprint arrived again and REJECT_DUPLICATE refused a new run. Look at the fixer's PR: did it land, and did it really fix the failing job?

remember: Name the fixer's run after the problem, not the build: one fingerprint, one run; new red builds join it as signals, and a problem that comes back after its run closed goes to a person.
